title: Kendra's 100-Meter Times
preview: Kendra wants her PR-impressive measure for her 100m times. Mean or median? Defend the honest answer.

body.goal: Compute mean and median for a small dataset and reason about which is more representative — even when it's not the one that 'looks fast.'
body.studentPrompt:
Kendra has run the 100-meter dash 7 times this season. Her times in seconds:

| Run | Time (sec) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 13.5 |
| 2 | 14.0 |
| 3 | 13.7 |
| 4 | 12.9 |
| 5 | 13.6 |
| 6 | 19.2 |
| 7 | 13.4 |

She wants to put **one number** on her sports résumé to describe how fast she is.

1. Compute the **mean** of her times. Show your work.
2. Compute the **median** of her times. Show your work.
3. Which measure should Kendra put on her résumé to describe her TYPICAL speed? Which one makes her look FASTER? Defend the difference.
4. Run 6 was 19.2 — way slower than the rest. What happened to mean vs median when Kendra removes Run 6 from the data? Recompute both and explain WHY one barely changed and one shifted a lot.
body.launch: Drop the times on the board. Don't talk about outliers — let them notice Run 6 and argue.
body.btcFit: Run 6 is a clear outlier (probably tripped, false start). Surfaces the mean vs median sensitivity argument.
body.anticipatedApproaches:
- Sorted: 12.9, 13.4, 13.5, 13.6, 13.7, 14.0, 19.2.
- Mean: (12.9 + 13.4 + 13.5 + 13.6 + 13.7 + 14.0 + 19.2) / 7 = 100.3 / 7 ≈ 14.33 sec.
- Median: middle value = 13.6 sec.
- Honest: 13.6 is more typical. Mean of 14.33 makes her look slower than she is because of the outlier.
- Remove Run 6: new mean (12.9+13.4+13.5+13.6+13.7+14.0)/6 = 81.1/6 ≈ 13.52. New median: midpoint of 13.5 and 13.6 = 13.55. Mean shifted from 14.33 → 13.52 (big change). Median barely shifted (13.6 → 13.55).
body.commonMisconceptions:
- 'Pick the smaller number for the résumé.' Honest vs marketing tension — the median is the honest typical here.
- 'Outliers don't matter because they're just one data point.' Mean is very sensitive to outliers; have them prove it.
body.discussionQuestions:
- When IS the mean a better summary than the median?
- If Kendra had 100 runs instead of 7, would one slow run affect the mean as much?
body.extensions: Sketch a dot plot of Kendra's times. Mark mean and median on it. Now invent a NEW dataset of 7 times where mean and median are exactly equal. How did you do it?
body.sampleSolutions:
**Q1.** Mean = (12.9 + 13.4 + 13.5 + 13.6 + 13.7 + 14.0 + 19.2) / 7 = 100.3 / 7 ≈ **14.33 sec**.

**Q2.** Sort: 12.9, 13.4, 13.5, **13.6**, 13.7, 14.0, 19.2. Median = **13.6 sec**.

**Q3.** **Median (13.6)** is more honest — it matches her typical performance. **Mean (14.33)** is dragged up by Run 6. She should put 13.6 on the résumé; the mean would make her look slower than she actually is.

**Q4.** Remove Run 6:

| Measure | With Run 6 | Without Run 6 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mean | 14.33 | 13.52 | −0.81 (big) |
| Median | 13.6 | 13.55 | −0.05 (tiny) |

The mean is much more sensitive to outliers because every value gets averaged in. The median only cares about the middle value(s) — Run 6 sitting at the top doesn't change which value is in the middle.
